subject: chemistry
title: Using materials (chemistry only)
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Using materials (chemistry only) — AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification, section 4.10.3.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry (AQA) practice covering Using materials (chemistry only), specification section 4.10.3.
final_note: You worked through Using materials (chemistry only) — 26 specification statements.

concepts.def: The destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment. It is a chemical change, not simply wear, and it is not limited to metals.
The corrosion of iron. Rusting is an example of corrosion, and both air and water are necessary for iron to rust: remove either one and no rust forms.
A layer applied to a metal that keeps air and water away from the metal surface, so corrosion cannot happen. Greasing, painting and electroplating are the examples the specification gives.
Covering the surface of one metal with a thin layer of another metal. In this topic it matters only as a way of putting a barrier coating onto a metal to prevent corrosion.

Aluminium has an oxide coating that protects the metal from further corrosion. The layer forms on the surface, stays firmly attached and stops air and water reaching the aluminium underneath, so the metal behaves as though it were unreactive.

Protecting a metal by putting it in contact with a more reactive metal. The more reactive metal corrodes in preference to the metal being protected, and it goes on doing so even where the coating is scratched or broken.
Coating iron with zinc. Zinc is more reactive than iron, so a galvanised coating acts both as a barrier and as sacrificial protection.
Water that has been boiled to drive out dissolved air and then covered with a layer of oil to stop air dissolving back in. It is the control used to test whether air is necessary for rusting.
A substance that absorbs water vapour. Sealed in a tube with an iron nail, it leaves the nail surrounded by dry air, which is the control used to test whether water is necessary for rusting.
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements. Most metals in everyday use are alloys rather than pure metals.
An alloy of copper and tin. It is used for statues, bells, medals and ornaments.
An alloy of copper and zinc. It is used for musical instruments such as trumpets and horns, and for taps, door fittings and other fixtures.
Gold used as jewellery is usually an alloy with silver, copper and zinc, because pure gold is too soft to wear well. Jewellery is the use to recall for this alloy.
The measure of the proportion of gold in a gold alloy, on a scale of 24. 24 carat is 100% gold (pure gold) and 18 carat is 75% gold.
An alloy of iron that contains specific amounts of carbon and other metals. Changing how much carbon and which other metals are present changes the properties of the steel.
Steel with a higher proportion of carbon. It is strong but brittle, which suits it to cutting tools and blades.
Steel with a lower proportion of carbon. It is softer and more easily shaped, which suits it to sheet products such as car body panels.
Steel containing chromium and nickel. Stainless steels are hard and resistant to corrosion, which suits them to cutlery, sinks and chemical plant.
An alloy of aluminium. Aluminium alloys are low density, which is why they are chosen for aircraft bodies and bicycle frames where weight matters.
The glass used for most everyday purposes, made by heating a mixture of sand, sodium carbonate and limestone.
Glass made from sand and boron trioxide. It melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass, which is why it is chosen where glass must be heated.
A material such as pottery or brick, made by shaping wet clay and then heating it in a furnace. The clay is fired, not melted.
The small molecule that polymer chains are built from. The properties of a polymer depend on what monomers it is made from and on the conditions under which it is made.
Low density poly(ethene), produced from the monomer ethene under one set of catalyst and reaction conditions. It is the less dense and more flexible of the two forms.
High density poly(ethene), produced from the same monomer, ethene, but using a different catalyst and different reaction conditions. It is the denser and stiffer of the two forms.
A polymer that melts when it is heated. Its structure is separate polymer chains, tangled together but not joined to each other, so heating lets the chains move apart.
A polymer that does not melt when it is heated. Its chains are joined to each other by cross-links, so the chains cannot move apart and the material keeps its shape when hot.
A material made of two materials: a matrix or binder surrounding and binding together fibres or fragments of the other material.
The continuous material in a composite that surrounds the reinforcement and binds it together, such as the cement in concrete or the resin in fibreglass.
The fibres or fragments held within the matrix of a composite, such as the gravel in concrete or the glass fibres in fibreglass.
A composite of glass fibres as the reinforcement held in a matrix of polymer resin. It is an example to recall, along with concrete and carbon fibre.
A composite in which fragments of gravel and sand are the reinforcement, bound together by a matrix of cement. Wood is an example of a natural composite.

A measurable property such as density, strength, hardness or melting point. Given data for glass and clay ceramics, polymers, composites and metals, these values are compared to explain uses and to select an appropriate material.

mcqs.q: What is meant by corrosion?
options: Damage that only metals suffer, caused by the air around them
Destruction of a material by chemical reactions with substances around it
The rusting of any metal that is left standing in air and water
Gradual wearing away of a surface by scratching, rubbing and use
mcqs.explain: This is the definition: corrosion is the destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment.

mcqs.q: Which conditions are necessary for iron to rust?
options: Water alone; the air makes no difference
Salt water, or water that contains an acid
Both air and water in contact with the iron
Air alone, provided the iron is left warm
mcqs.explain: The specification states that both air and water are necessary for iron to rust.

mcqs.q: Three iron nails are sealed in tubes. Tube 1: nail in tap water, open to air. Tube 2: nail in water that has been boiled, covered by a layer of oil. Tube 3: nail in dry air over anhydrous calcium chloride. Only the nail in tube 1 rusts. What does the result for tube 2 show?
options: Water is not necessary, since this nail was wet and did not rust
Air is necessary, since the wet nail did not rust without it
The oil layer is what stopped this nail from rusting
Boiling the water made the rusting reaction much slower
mcqs.explain: Boiling removes dissolved air and the oil stops it returning, so tube 2 has water but no air, and no rust forms.

mcqs.q: In the rusting experiment, why is anhydrous calcium chloride sealed in the tube with one of the nails?
options: It absorbs the air, so only water can reach the nail
It coats the nail in a barrier that keeps out damp
It speeds up rusting, so a result is seen sooner
It absorbs water vapour, so the nail is left in dry air
mcqs.explain: Removing water while leaving air present is the control that tests whether water is necessary for rusting.

mcqs.q: Greasing, painting and electroplating all prevent corrosion. How do they work?
options: They make the metal underneath much less reactive
They replace an oxide layer that has flaked off the metal
They form a barrier that keeps air and water off the metal
They react with the metal to form a harder new compound
mcqs.explain: All three are barrier coatings: they separate the metal surface from the substances that would attack it.

mcqs.q: Aluminium is high in the reactivity series, yet aluminium window frames do not corrode away. Why not?
options: Aluminium is unreactive, so air and water do not attack it
Its oxide flakes away, leaving fresh metal that is tougher
An oxide coating forms that protects the metal underneath
Aluminium is always painted before it is used outdoors
mcqs.explain: Aluminium has an oxide coating that stays attached and protects the metal from further corrosion.

mcqs.q: Iron is galvanised by coating it with which metal?
options: Zinc
Tin
Chromium
Copper
mcqs.explain: Zinc is used to galvanise iron; it is more reactive than iron and so protects it sacrificially.

mcqs.q: Why does a zinc coating go on protecting iron even after the coating has been scratched through?
options: Zinc is less reactive, so air and water do not attack it
The scratch seals itself as the soft zinc spreads into it
The zinc makes the iron beneath it less reactive than before
Zinc is more reactive, so the zinc corrodes instead of iron
mcqs.explain: Sacrificial protection: the more reactive metal is attacked in preference, so exposed iron is still protected.

mcqs.q: Blocks of magnesium are bolted to the steel hull of a ship. Why does this protect the steel?
options: Magnesium is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes first
Magnesium is less reactive than iron, so it resists the sea
Any metal bolted to a hull will corrode before the steel does
The blocks spread out and seal the hull against the seawater
mcqs.explain: Sacrificial protection explained by relative reactivity: the more reactive magnesium is attacked instead of the iron.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the metals in everyday use is correct?
options: Most are compounds, formed when metals react together
Most are pure metals, refined to remove everything else
Most are pure metals with a thin coat of a second metal
Most are alloys, which are mixtures containing a metal
mcqs.explain: Most metals in everyday use are alloys, and an alloy is a mixture rather than a compound.

mcqs.q: Which statement about bronze and brass is correct?
options: Bronze is copper with zinc; brass is copper with tin
Both are compounds made when copper reacts with a metal
Both are pure copper that has been hardened by heating
Bronze is copper with tin; brass is copper with zinc
mcqs.explain: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin, and brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.

mcqs.q: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Which use is it best matched to?
options: Statues and bells, which are cast from copper and tin
Musical instruments such as trumpets, and taps and fittings
Cutting blades and tools, which must be hard and brittle
Aircraft panels, which need the lowest possible density
mcqs.explain: Brass is the alloy used for brass instruments and for taps, door fittings and similar fixtures.

mcqs.q: A gold ring is sold as 18 carat. What does that tell you?
options: It is 18% gold, the rest being silver and copper
It has a mass of 18 carats, a unit used for gold
It is 75% gold, alloyed with silver, copper and zinc
It is gold that has been mixed with 18 other metals
mcqs.explain: The carat scale runs to 24 for pure gold, and the specification gives 18 carat as 75% gold.

mcqs.q: A bracelet is 12 carat gold. What percentage of it is gold?
mcqs.explain: 24 carat is 100% gold, so 12 carat is 12 out of 24, which is 50%.

mcqs.q: How do high carbon steel and low carbon steel differ?
options: High carbon steel is strong but brittle; low carbon is softer
High carbon steel is stronger in every way and will not break
High carbon steel is pure iron; low carbon steel is an alloy
Low carbon steel resists corrosion; high carbon steel does not
mcqs.explain: The specification states high carbon steel is strong but brittle, and low carbon steel is softer and more easily shaped.

mcqs.q: Stainless steels are hard and resistant to corrosion. What are they?
options: Iron that has been electroplated with a layer of chromium
A pure form of iron from which the carbon has been removed
Iron alloyed with tin, a metal that does not corrode in damp
Iron alloyed with chromium and nickel as well as carbon
mcqs.explain: Steels containing chromium and nickel are the stainless steels; the added metals are alloyed throughout.

mcqs.q: Car body panels are pressed into shape from flat sheet. Which steel is used, and why?
options: Low carbon steel, because it is softer and easily shaped
Stainless steel, because a chromium plating can never rust
High carbon steel, because it is much the strongest of them
High carbon steel, because brittle metals bend most easily
mcqs.explain: Pressing sheet into shape needs a steel that can be deformed without cracking, which is low carbon steel.

mcqs.q: Why are aluminium alloys, rather than steels, used for aircraft bodies?
options: Aluminium alloys are low density, so the aircraft is lighter
Aluminium is the strongest of all the metals used in industry
Aluminium is unreactive, so the body will never need a coating
Aluminium alloys melt at a higher temperature than all steels
mcqs.explain: Aluminium alloys are low density, which is the property that matters when mass must be lifted.

mcqs.q: A table gives two alloys. P: density 8.9 g/cm3, very hard, corrodes in damp air. Q: density 2.7 g/cm3, moderate strength, resists corrosion. Which is the better choice for a bicycle frame kept outdoors, and why?
options: P, because the hardest alloy always makes the best frame
Q, because it is far less dense and it resists corrosion
P, because a denser alloy is always the stronger of the two
Q, because low density is a sign of very high strength
mcqs.explain: A frame must be light and must survive outdoors, and the data show Q is better on both counts.

mcqs.q: Soda-lime glass is made by heating a mixture of which substances?
options: Sand, boron trioxide and limestone
Sand, sodium carbonate and limestone
Sand, sodium chloride and limestone
Sodium carbonate and boron trioxide
mcqs.explain: This is the mixture the specification gives for soda-lime glass.

mcqs.q: Why is borosilicate glass, rather than soda-lime glass, used for laboratory glassware that is heated?
options: It contains limestone, which stops the glass from melting
It melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass does
It is a composite, so its fibres hold the shape when hot
It is made from sand alone, so it has no impurities in it
mcqs.explain: The specification states that borosilicate glass melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass.

mcqs.q: How are clay ceramics such as bricks and pottery made?
options: Clay is melted and then poured into a cold metal mould
Dry clay powder is pressed hard, with no heating at all
Clay fibres are set into a matrix of cement or of resin
Wet clay is shaped, and then heated in a furnace
mcqs.explain: Clay ceramics are made by shaping wet clay and then heating it in a furnace.

mcqs.q: Low density and high density poly(ethene) are both produced from ethene. How can one monomer give two different materials?
options: The high density polymer is made from a heavier monomer
The high density polymer simply has much longer chains
The two are made using different catalysts and conditions
One of them is a composite of ethene held in a matrix
mcqs.explain: Properties of polymers depend on the monomers and on the conditions under which they are made, and here only the conditions differ.

mcqs.q: In terms of their structures, why do thermosetting polymers not melt when they are heated?
options: Their chains are far longer and heavier than in other plastics
The covalent bonds along their chains are much stronger ones
Their chains are held to each other by covalent cross-links
Their chains are packed more closely than in ordinary plastics
mcqs.explain: Cross-links between the chains stop the chains moving apart, so the material cannot melt.

mcqs.q: A plastic saucepan handle chars but does not soften when it is heated strongly. What does this show?
options: It is thermosetting, because such polymers do not melt
It is thermosoftening, but its chains are unusually long
It is thermosetting, but would melt if heated far hotter
It is a clay ceramic, since these are fired in a furnace
mcqs.explain: Thermosetting polymers do not melt when they are heated, so charring without softening identifies one.

mcqs.q: Most composites are made of two materials. What are the two parts called?
options: Two metals melted together to give a single mixture
A matrix or binder surrounding a reinforcement
Fibres that surround and bind fragments of the matrix
A coating on the outside and the material underneath
mcqs.explain: A matrix or binder surrounds and binds together fibres or fragments of the reinforcement.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a composite material?
options: Concrete: fragments of gravel bound by cement
Wool: natural fibres twisted together into yarn
Brass: copper and zinc melted to form a mixture
Pottery: wet clay shaped and fired in a furnace
mcqs.explain: Cement is the matrix and the gravel fragments are the reinforcement, which fits the definition exactly.

mcqs.q: A table gives densities in g/cm3: steel 7.9, aluminium alloy 2.7, fibreglass 1.9, poly(ethene) 0.94. All of them are stiffer than poly(ethene). A part must be as light as possible but stiffer than a polymer. Which should be chosen?
options: Poly(ethene), because 0.94 g/cm3 is the lowest density listed
Steel, because at 7.9 g/cm3 the densest is always the stiffest
Fibreglass, at 1.9 g/cm3 and stiffer than the polymer
Steel, because the strongest material given is the safest pick
mcqs.explain: Of the materials that meet the stiffness condition, fibreglass has the lowest density in the table.

mcqs.q: A saucepan handle must not melt, must not conduct heat well, and must be moulded cheaply in quantity. Which material is most appropriate?
options: A thermosoftening polymer, which softens only when charred
Stainless steel, the hardest and strongest of the choices
A clay ceramic, melted and poured into the shape needed
A thermosetting polymer, which does not melt when heated
mcqs.explain: It meets every requirement: it does not melt, polymers are poor thermal conductors, and it can be moulded.
